name: The World of AI: AI Laws by State tracker and comparison
title: The World of AI: AI Laws by State tracker and comparison
answer: This is The World of AI's AI Laws page, a daily tracker of US state artificial intelligence legislation. It reports 6,003 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, sourced from LegiScan, and a September 18, 2026 review of 101 enrolled measures across 27 states. Its most useful finding is that no two states wrote the same law, yet common duties recur: tell people when they deal with AI, keep a qualified person in decisions about health, employment, benefits or education, and expect attorneys general to enforce the larger laws.

sections.body: The World of AI publishes this AI Laws page. It is a reference and tracking page, not a bill text or legal advice document. It covers United States state artificial intelligence legislation across 53 jurisdictions, with 6,003 AI bills refreshed daily from the LegiScan legislative database and linked to each bill's official page. It also describes a comparison of enrolled text from 101 measures across 27 states, reviewed on September 18, 2026. The page says every page is rebuilt daily from primary sources and carries the date it was last verified.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page says United States AI legislation is written state by state, and it tracks 6,003 artificial intelligence bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from LegiScan. It also reports a comparison built from enrolled text of each AI measure a state has passed, covering 101 measures across 27 states and reviewed on September 18, 2026. No two states wrote the same law, but the same choices keep appearing. Only two states passed a broad law reaching consequential decisions across sectors, Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149. Every other measure names one setting, such as a companion chatbot, a political ad, an insurance prior authorization, a classroom or a state agency. Where stakes are personal, legislatures keep writing the same rule: AI may assist, but it may not be the only decider. Insurers cannot deny care on an algorithm alone, AI cannot deliver therapy or present itself as a licensed clinician, it cannot be the sole instructor of a college course or score a teacher evaluation, and New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions. No state created a new agency to enforce AI law. The attorney general enforces the larger laws. Tell people when they are dealing with AI, keep a qualified person in decisions about health, employment, benefits or education, have a crisis protocol and know the age of your user if your product holds a conversation, and keep records because the attorney general is the enforcer you are most likely to meet.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states 6,003 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily from LegiScan. It states 101 measures across 27 states, reviewed on September 18, 2026. It states only Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149 passed broad laws reaching consequential decisions across sectors. It states no state created a new agency to enforce AI law, the attorney general enforces the larger laws often exclusively, and several states declare a violation an unfair or deceptive trade practice under their consumer protection act. It names AL SB63 and IA HF2635 for insurer care denials, IL HB1806, TN HB1470 and CA AB489 for therapy or licensed clinician limits, IL HB1859 and IL SB2909 for college instruction and teacher evaluation, and NY S07599 for human review before agencies automate benefit decisions. It also lists enforcement examples CA SB53, CO SB189, GA SB540, ID S1297, IL SB0315, NY S06953, RI H7350 and TX HB149, and consumer protection examples CT HB05222, HI SB3001, ME LD1727, TN HB1470 and WA HB2225.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in Government would use this source to see the state legislative patchwork that public agencies and contractors face. It shows which states have passed AI measures, what settings those measures cover, and where duties recur, such as human review before agencies automate benefit decisions in New York and limits on AI as the sole decider in health, therapy, education and employment. It also shows that attorneys general, not new AI agencies, are the main enforcers, with sector regulators handling insurance, licensing and elections. That makes it useful for policy, procurement, compliance and oversight planning across states.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Government

sections.body: The source text focuses on state AI legislation. It is a tracker and comparison, not a full legal analysis, and it does not cover implementation, court outcomes or local rules beyond the tracked bills. The comparison is dated September 18, 2026, while the tracker says it is refreshed daily. The page also carries promotional material for books and consulting services by Stephen R. Jordan, including an AI novel and audit services, so it is not a purely neutral publisher.
